vo_parts.text: Field report: the PCB Gold-Master Eval.

scenes.vo: This is the memory bus of a DDR5 test board, routed by hand. Every serpentine is an engineer matching lengths to fractions of a millimetre. Machine-learning routers are judged on wirelength and design-rule checks. None of those scores sees this.

Thirty sources were graded. Search beats reinforcement learning per dollar, so far. In the one independent rerun of Google's chip placer, reinforcement learning used twenty-one times the CPU-hours of simulated annealing, for equal or worse results. And no learned PCB method optimises signal integrity end to end.

The open-source stack is nearly complete. KiCad, Freerouting and KiCad Routing Tools to route. Open E M S and Antmicro's gerber-to-E M S for physics. Evolutionary and L L M-driven optimisers to search. The missing piece is fast, faithful physics.

So the eval comes first. Eight boards Antmicro built and open-sourced, from a four-layer test board to twelve-layer DDR5 testers. Each task strips the copper, asks an agent to route it, and scores the result against the human original: completion, design rules, pair skew, length matching and impedance-correct widths. The human copper scores itself a perfect one, on all eight boards.

The open-source router connects the board, and misses the physics. On the M.2 PCIe adapter it made ninety-two per cent of the connections, but only one pair in nine met the skew target. Reward: zero point two five, out of one.

A forecast built from published scaling results and measured costs says compute is cheap: a routing candidate costs about a cent. Below a few hundred dollars per board, wall-clock time and the evaluator decide the outcome. Spend on parallel CPU and on the evaluator. Buy GPUs only after the solver earns them.
Measure the physics. Search before you learn. Keep the human copper as the answer key.
